about: Every spacecraft operating at Mars (orbiters, rovers) as of mid-November 2026, plus recently ended surface/orbit missions (Ingenuity, InSight, MAVEN, Mars Orbiter Mission), the silent Zhurong rover, and spacecraft en route (ESCAPADE twins, MMX). Older ended missions (Viking, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, MGS, etc.) are out of scope. Status is taken from the latest source found by 2026-11-18. 'status_as_of' is the date of that source, not a confirmation on 2026-11-18. Coordinates are planetocentric latitude N and east longitude (-180..180), mostly from Wikipedia. Orbit altitudes are above the surface and are nominal or approximate: orbits drift and are sometimes adjusted. Masses are labelled launch/wet or dry. Distances driven are odometry figures from NASA with their date. Agencies rarely announce 'still alive', so 'Active' means the latest dated source shows the spacecraft operating. See each row's 'uncertain' for weak spots. ESCAPADE and MMX are on their way (MMX goes to Phobos). Ingenuity's final site has no sourced coordinates, so it is not on the map. 'source' is the main source of each row, 'more_sources' the others (space separated).
not_included: Rosalind Franklin (ESA ExoMars rover): launch planned 2028, not at Mars.
Mars Telecommunications Orbiter (NASA): planned to join the relay network around 2028.
Tianwen-3 (China, Mars sample return): launch planned around 2028.
Older ended missions (Viking 1/2, Mars Pathfinder, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, Mars Global Surveyor, Beagle 2, Schiaparelli, Mars Polar Lander, etc.): out of scope.

missions.name: Perseverance
missions.status_note: Operating. Set the off-world driving record on 2026-10-11 (sol 2006). Its extended mission began October 2026 and runs to about the end of 2028.
missions.site: Octavia E. Butler Landing, Jezero crater
missions.now_at: Lac de Charmes, off the western rim of Jezero crater, heading to the target 'Idubi'; 45.22 km driven by 2026-10-11
missions.instruments: Mastcam-Z, SuperCam, PIXL, SHERLOC (with WATSON), RIMFAX, MEDA, MOXIE
missions.goal: Look for signs of ancient microbial life in Jezero crater's former lake and river deposits, and cache rock samples for possible return to Earth.
missions.highlight: On 2026-10-11 its odometer read 45.22 km, passing Opportunity's 45.16 km off-world record in about 5.5 years (Opportunity took nearly 15). More than 90% of the distance was driven with AutoNav.
missions.uncertain: Distance is as of 2026-10-11; the mid-November total is somewhat higher. Current coordinates were not sourced. The mass is dry rover mass; the launch mass of the whole Mars 2020 spacecraft is not given here.

missions.name: Curiosity
missions.status_note: Operating. The mission blog for sols 5063-5069 (planned 2026-11-06) describes finishing a drill campaign at the 'Nazca' hole, then driving back to its southerly route on Mount Sharp.
missions.site: Bradbury Landing, Aeolis Palus, Gale crater
missions.now_at: Lower slopes of Mount Sharp (Aeolis Mons), Gale crater; 38.07 km driven by 2026-10-11
missions.instruments: Mastcam, ChemCam, MAHLI, MARDI, APXS, CheMin, SAM, RAD, DAN, REMS
missions.goal: Find out whether Gale crater ever offered environments that could support microbial life, by reading the layered rocks of Mount Sharp.
missions.highlight: It landed less than 2.4 km from the centre of its target after a trip of about 560 million km, and has worked in Gale crater for more than 5,000 sols.
missions.uncertain: Distance sources disagree. NASA gives 38.07 km as of 2026-10-11 (used here). Wikipedia's infobox gives 38.16 km as of 2026-10-30, and its text gives 36.86 km, which is likely a different measure (straight-line distance from the landing site, or an older figure). Current coordinates were not sourced.

missions.name: Ingenuity
missions.mission: Mars Helicopter (technology demonstration, carried by Mars 2020)
missions.status_note: Flight 72 on 2024-01-18 damaged its rotor blades on landing at Airfield Chi in the Valinor Hills. NASA announced the end of its flight mission on 2024-01-25. It then stayed on the ground as a stationary weather and data station; that role is not tracked here.
missions.site: Wright Brothers Field, Jezero crater (deployed 2021-04-03; first flight 2021-04-19). Final resting place: Airfield Chi, Valinor Hills, Jezero crater.
missions.now_at: Airfield Chi, Valinor Hills, Jezero crater (resting since 2024-01-18)
missions.instruments: RTE colour camera, NAV black-and-white camera
missions.goal: Show that powered, controlled flight is possible in Mars's thin atmosphere. It later served as an aerial scout for Perseverance.
missions.highlight: It was planned for up to 5 test flights in 30 days and flew 72 times over almost three years.
missions.uncertain: Launch and arrival dates are those of Mars 2020, under which it travelled. Final-site coordinates were not sourced. Its 'planned 5 flights' comes from general knowledge of the mission and was not rechecked here.

missions.name: InSight
missions.mission: Interior Exploration using Seismic Investigations, Geodesy and Heat Transport
missions.status_note: Dust on its solar panels cut its power. Last contact was 2022-12-15, and NASA declared the mission over on 2022-12-21.
missions.goal: Measure Mars's interior structure (crust, mantle, core) with a seismometer, heat-flow probe and radio-science geodesy.
missions.highlight: It recorded 1,313 marsquakes (count as of May 2022). A 2024 analysis of its seismic data pointed to liquid water about 10-20 km down in the crust.
missions.uncertain: The marsquake count may differ slightly in the final catalogue. The 'liquid water' result is one interpretation (Wright et al. 2024), not a consensus.

missions.name: Zhurong
missions.status_note: It went into planned hibernation on 2022-05-18 ahead of dust storms and winter. It was expected to wake around December 2022 but never did. NASA HiRISE images showed it had not moved from September 2022 to February 2023. In April 2023 the chief designer Zhang Rongqiao blamed heavy dust on the solar panels and said it might stay inactive 'forever'. No later recovery or formal end-of-mission announcement was found.
missions.now_at: Southern Utopia Planitia, about 1.9 km south of its landing site (stationary since May 2022)
missions.instruments: RoPeR (ground-penetrating radar), RoMAG (magnetometer), MCS (climate station), MarSCoDe (composition), MSCam (multispectral camera), NaTeCam (navigation & terrain cameras)
missions.goal: Study the geology, soil, subsurface layers and climate of southern Utopia Planitia. It was China's first Mars rover.
missions.highlight: It was planned to work 90 sols and operated for about a year (May 2021 to May 2022). With it, China became the second country to drive a rover on Mars.
missions.uncertain: No 2024-2026 statement from CNSA was found, so the status 'dormant' rests on 2023 reports and continued silence. The exact date of last contact was not found: hibernation began 2022-05-18. The odometry date is 5 or 6 May 2022 (Wikipedia gives both). The 'second country to drive a rover' fact is general knowledge, not rechecked here.

missions.name: Tianwen-1 orbiter
missions.status_note: Imaged interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS from Mars orbit on 2025-09-30 to 10-03. In an article of 2026-05-20, NAOC researcher Ren Xin said this shows the orbiter is 'operating stably and in good condition'. Social media claimed it lost contact in April 2026 and would retire on 2026-09-24, but no official source confirms this.
missions.orbit: near-polar elliptical remote-sensing orbit, ~275 x 10,749 km, 86.3 deg, period ~7.08 h
missions.instruments: MoRIC, HiRIC, MOSIR (radar), MMS (mineralogy spectrometer), MOMAG (magnetometer), MINPA (ion & neutral analyser), MEPA (energetic particles)
missions.goal: Map Mars globally (topography, geology, minerals, subsurface ice, space environment) and relay data for the Zhurong rover.
missions.mass_note: orbiter launch mass (the whole Tianwen-1 spacecraft was about 5,000 kg)
missions.highlight: Its high-resolution camera, built to photograph the bright Martian surface, imaged the faint interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS from about 30 million km away.
missions.uncertain: Status is the least certain of the 'Active' rows. The 2026-05-20 quote is about observations made in 2025, and no CNSA status release from 2026 was found. The rumour of loss of contact and retirement on 2026-09-24 is unconfirmed. Wikipedia's text gives a periapsis of about 265 km against 275 km in its table. The current orbit may have been adjusted since.

missions.name: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter
missions.status_note: Operating, and the main high-rate relay for Curiosity and Perseverance. HiRISE passed 100,000 images around December 2025 and is ageing. CRISM was retired on 2023-04-03. In January 2024 it had about 132 kg of fuel left, enough to about 2035.
missions.orbit: near-polar, sun-synchronous (~3 pm local time), ~250 x 316 km, ~93 deg, period ~112 min
missions.instruments: HiRISE, CTX, MARCI, CRISM (retired 2023), MCS, SHARAD
missions.goal: Map Mars in high resolution, trace the history of water and climate, and relay data from surface missions.
missions.highlight: It helped choose the landing sites for Phoenix, Curiosity, InSight and Perseverance, and in 2015 HiRISE found the lost Beagle 2 lander on the surface.
missions.uncertain: No single NASA release from November 2026 was found. 'Active' rests on 2026 HiRISE imaging (for example of Perseverance's record drive) and relay reporting. The orbit altitudes are the nominal 2006 science orbit, and the current figures may differ slightly. The '~3 pm' local time is general knowledge, not rechecked.

missions.name: MAVEN
missions.status_note: Contact was lost on 2025-12-06 after it passed behind Mars. A review board found it in safe mode and spinning unusually fast, which drained the batteries and cut power to its radio. NASA declared the mission over on 2026-06-03 after about six months of failed recovery attempts. The root cause is still under investigation, with a final report expected later in 2026. The dead spacecraft is expected to stay in orbit for 50-100 years.
missions.orbit: elliptical, ~75 deg inclination, period ~3.6 h. After 2019 aerobraking, ~130 km x ~4,500 km.
missions.instruments: IUVS, NGIMS, SWIA, SWEA, STATIC, SEP, LPW (with EUV monitor), MAG
missions.goal: Measure how Mars loses its upper atmosphere to space, to explain how the planet changed from wet to dry.
missions.highlight: It showed that the solar wind strips gas from Mars's upper atmosphere, a main reason the planet lost most of its air. It also relayed rover data until its loss.
missions.uncertain: Orbit figures conflict. Wikipedia's infobox gives 180 x 4,500 km, while its text says 2019 aerobraking lowered periapsis to about 130 km. The orbit at loss may also have been disturbed by the spin. The root cause is not yet published. The fun fact paraphrases MAVEN's well-known headline result and was not quoted from a source fetched here.

missions.name: Mars Odyssey
missions.status_note: Still operating in 2026, though near the end of its fuel. NASA's 2023 estimate (about 4 kg of hydrazine) covered operations 'through at least the end of 2025'. Wikipedia says it was still collecting data as of April 2026, and lists 'last contact: 2026 (planned)'. The team marked 25 years since launch on 2026-04-15. NASA's relay page (June 2026) still lists it as a relay orbiter, now a backup with 0-1 relay passes a day. Congress restored its funding in January 2026 after the White House proposed ending it.
missions.orbit: near-polar, sun-synchronous, ~400 km roughly circular, ~93.1 deg, period ~2 h
missions.instruments: THEMIS, GRS suite (GRS, NS, HEND), MARIE (failed 2003)
missions.goal: Map the minerals, subsurface hydrogen (water ice) and radiation environment of Mars, and relay data from landers and rovers.
missions.highlight: It is the longest-working spacecraft at another planet (record held since December 2010), with more than 100,000 orbits. In 2002 it found the hydrogen signature of shallow water ice at high latitudes.
missions.uncertain: This is the row most likely to change soon. No NASA source from after mid-2026 confirms contact, and Wikipedia's 'last contact: 2026 (planned)' suggests a planned end in 2026; no announced end date was found. The orbit is approximate (Wikipedia gives about 400 km) and the local time has been drifting. The 'water ice found in 2002' fact is general mission history, not rechecked here.

missions.name: Mars Express
missions.status_note: Operating. It is confirmed through 2026-12-31. ESA's Science Programme Committee approved an indicative extension from 2027-01-01 to 2028-12-31 (in part to support JAXA's MMX), and the team requested funding to 2029. A May 2025 gyroscope software update could keep it working to about 2034. 2026 science papers and abstracts show it is still working. Its Beagle 2 lander was lost on arrival in 2003.
missions.orbit: highly elliptical, near-polar, ~298 x 10,107 km, 86.3 deg, period ~6.7-7.5 h
missions.instruments: HRSC, OMEGA, MARSIS, PFS, SPICAM, ASPERA-3, MaRS, VMC
missions.goal: Study Mars's atmosphere, surface and subsurface from orbit, from 3D colour mapping to radar searches for buried water ice.
missions.mass_note: launch mass, including Beagle 2 (dry mass 666 kg)
missions.highlight: It was planned as a two-year mission and is now in its third decade. Its MARSIS radar reported signs of liquid water beneath the south polar ice (2018), a result that is still debated.
missions.uncertain: Whether ESA has confirmed the 2027-2028 extension (expected at the late-2026 ministerial-level budget decisions) was not found. Wikipedia gives a period of 7.5 h in its infobox and 6.7 h in its text, and a launch mass of 1,123 kg in one place and 1,223 kg in another. The MARSIS subglacial-water claim is disputed in the literature.

missions.name: ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter
missions.status_note: Operating. Its 2025 observations include comet 3I/ATLAS (CaSSIS, 2025-10-03), and Wikipedia lists results published through 2026-11-04. It also relays data for NASA rovers and is planned to relay for ESA's Rosalind Franklin rover (launch planned 2028). Its Schiaparelli lander crashed on 2016-10-19 after its parachute was released too early.
missions.orbit: near-circular, ~400 km, 74 deg inclination, period ~2 h
missions.goal: Make a detailed inventory of trace gases in the Martian atmosphere (especially methane), and map subsurface water ice and surface features.
missions.mass_note: orbiter wet mass (4,332 kg at launch with Schiaparelli)
missions.highlight: Its very sensitive spectrometers found no methane in the upper atmosphere and set strict upper limits, which deepened the puzzle of the methane Curiosity detects at the surface.
missions.uncertain: A 2024 abstract said its funding was in place only to the end of 2025, and no official ESA document on its 2026+ extension was found, although 2026 publications show it still working. The orbit is the nominal science orbit. The comparison with Curiosity's surface methane is interpretation and paraphrased.

missions.name: Hope
missions.status_note: Operating. On 2026-02-17 the UAE Space Agency extended the mission to 2028, to study how the lower and upper atmosphere are linked over another Martian year.
missions.orbit: high elliptical, ~20,000 x 43,000 km, 25 deg inclination, period ~55 h (sees the whole disk at all local times)
missions.goal: Build the first full picture of Martian weather and the atmosphere through the day and across seasons, from the lower atmosphere to the escaping upper layers.
missions.mass_note: launch mass incl. ~800 kg fuel (dry mass 550 kg)
missions.highlight: It was the Arab world's first interplanetary mission. In March 2023 it took the closest-ever images of the far side of the moon Deimos.
missions.uncertain: The launch was 2020-07-19 at 21:58 UTC, which was 2020-07-20 local UAE/Japan time; sources differ on which date to use. The orbit values are nominal and approximate. The 'closest-ever images of Deimos' wording is paraphrased from Wikipedia's summary of the 2023 flyby.

missions.name: Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan)
missions.status_note: Contact was lost around April 2022, probably when a long eclipse drained its battery and fuel ran out. The loss was reported on 2022-10-02, and ISRO declared the orbiter unrecoverable the next day.
missions.orbit: highly elliptical, ~421.7 x 76,993.6 km, 150 deg inclination (retrograde)
missions.goal: Demonstrate India's ability to reach Mars orbit, and study the surface and upper atmosphere with five small instruments.
missions.highlight: It made India the first Asian nation to reach Mars orbit, on its first attempt, for about US$73 million.
missions.uncertain: The exact day of last contact (April 2022) is not known. The orbit values are from early in the mission and changed later. 'First attempt' is general knowledge, not rechecked here.

missions.name: ESCAPADE (Blue and Gold)
missions.mission: Escape and Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorers
missions.agency: NASA (SIMPLEx); UC Berkeley SSL (lead), Rocket Lab (spacecraft)
missions.status_note: Launched on Blue Origin's New Glenn (NG-2). Both spacecraft then waited for a year in a loiter orbit near Sun-Earth L2. Powered Earth flybys on 2026-11-07 (Blue) and 2026-11-09 (Gold) sent them toward Mars. Mars orbit insertion is planned for September 2027, a few days apart, followed by about six months of lowering the orbit. Science orbit is expected by mid-2028.
missions.orbit: Planned science orbit (Campaign A): ~170 x 8,400 km, ~65 deg, period ~5.66 h, both on the same orbit. Campaign B: Blue apoapsis 7,000 km, Gold 10,000 km. Not at Mars yet.
missions.instruments: EMAG (magnetometer), EESA (electrostatic analyser), ELP (Langmuir probe), VISIONS (camera)
missions.goal: Use two spacecraft to measure, at the same time and in two places, how the solar wind drives the escape of Mars's upper atmosphere.
missions.highlight: It is the first NASA mission sent to Mars by a powered Earth flyby after a year-long wait near L2, a flexible approach that frees Mars missions from the 26-month launch window.
missions.uncertain: Its arrival is planned for September 2027, with no exact date found. Sources differ on the inclination (~65 deg in Wikipedia's text, 60 deg in its infobox) and on the closest Earth-flyby distance (about 600 km vs 1,046-1,609 km). The 'frees missions from the launch window' wording paraphrases NASA's framing.

missions.name: MMX
missions.agency: JAXA (with CNES, DLR, NASA, ESA contributions)
missions.status_note: Launched on H3 Flight 10 from Tanegashima at 04:41:03 JST on 2026-10-20 (19:41 UTC on 2026-10-19). JAXA reported first contact after launch (news item of 2026-10-26). The cruise takes about one year, so it arrives in the Mars system around 2027. Phobos operations are planned for 2027-2030, with the IDEFIX rover landing on Phobos around 2029 and about 10 g of Phobos samples to be returned to Earth.
missions.orbit: Not at Mars yet. Planned: Mars orbit, then quasi-satellite orbits around Phobos.
missions.instruments: TENGOO, OROCHI, LIDAR, MEGANE (GRS/NS), MIRS, CMDM, MSA, IREM, Sampler (C-SMP, P-SMP), IDEFIX rover, SHV camera
missions.goal: Find out where Phobos and Deimos came from (captured asteroids or debris from a giant impact) by returning the first samples from a Martian moon.
missions.highlight: If it succeeds, it will be the first sample-return mission from the Mars system.
missions.expected_arrival_text: August 2027 (planned Mars orbit insertion; no day announced)
missions.uncertain: The launch success is confirmed by JAXA's own MMX site; no independent news report was fetched. The exact Mars arrival date and the spacecraft mass were not sourced. It is a Phobos mission, so whether to show it as a 'Mars mission' is an editorial choice.
